Q1: Decision: dispatch the medic unit to Call A (Maple St, chest pain, 7.8). Call A is the highest-scored call the unit can handle, and chest pain in a 68-year-old is a potentially life-threatening time-sensitive emergency. Per the threshold rule, the 9.0 threshold never means holding units — an idle unit with calls waiting is a failure.
Q2: Decision: dispatch the engine to Call A (Pine Rd, kitchen fire, 8.4). It is the highest-scored call the engine can handle; a kitchen fire threatens the structure and remaining property even with the family evacuated. The 9.0 threshold does not justify holding the engine while a fire is burning.
Q3: Decision: dispatch the ladder truck to Call A (1st St, 8.9 — person trapped on 3rd floor, smoke showing). Call A edges out Call B on the urgency score, and the score is the tiebreaker by design; an entrapped person with smoke showing is an immediate life-safety priority. Call B (elevator rescue, 8.8) is queued second and gets the next available unit.
Q4: Decision: dispatch the BLS unit to Call A (Hill Rd, diabetic emergency, 7.1). It is the highest-scored call the unit can handle, and a diabetic emergency in a conscious patient can deteriorate quickly. Call B is an event standby (5.5) — a low-priority scheduled assignment that can wait behind a real medical call.
Q5: Decision: dispatch the medic unit to Call A (River St, difficulty breathing, 8.1). The scores are nearly tied but the score exists precisely as the tiebreaker, and Call A wins it; a breathing emergency is also more likely to deteriorate rapidly than a hip injury. Call B (8.0) stays queued for the next available unit.
Q6: Decision: dispatch the engine to Call A (Main St, vehicle fire, 6.8) and request the neighboring jurisdiction's mutual aid for Call B (Side St, brush fire near homes, 6.5). Call A is the highest-scored call the engine can handle, and mutual aid covers Call B so neither call waits on an idle unit. Brush fire near homes still gets timely coverage through the mutual aid request.
Q7: Decision: dispatch the battalion chief to Call A (Park Ave, multi-vehicle accident with injuries, 7.5). It is the only call waiting and it specifically needs command oversight; leaving a chief idle with a pending call needing command is exactly the empty-queue-with-idle-units failure. Dispatch now, manage command on scene.
Q8: Decision: dispatch the medic unit to Call A (Cedar Ln, stroke symptoms, 8.7). It is the highest-scored call the unit can handle, and the closing treatment window makes it genuinely time-critical — stroke outcomes degrade by the minute. Call B (abdominal pain, 7.3) is serious but stable enough to queue behind it.
Q9: Decision: dispatch the engine to Call A (Summit Dr, gas leak report, 5.9). It is the only call waiting; holding the engine because the score is low would put an idle unit next to an unmitigated gas leak, which the threshold rule explicitly forbids. Score only orders priority among multiple calls, never justifies inaction on a lone call.
